Mary Pelston
— The Fearless Kentucky Girl

Mary Eveline Pelston was born in Cumberland County, Kentucky, on March 1, 1926, married Edward Joseph Dedo in Chicago in 1944, and spent most of her adult life in North Riverside, Illinois. She died on April 22, 2014, and lies at Mount Emblem Cemetery in Elmhurst.

Kentucky beginnings

Her full name was Mary Eveline Pelston1. Proven She was the daughter of Carl Dolphus Pelston and Mary Pearl Branham2 of Cumberland County, Kentucky.14 Proven

Mary was born 1 March 1926 in Burkesville3, Cumberland County, Kentucky.

She grew up in a full house. The 1930 census shows Carl and Pearl's children in order: Buel, 13; Vernie Lee, 10; Clyde, 8; James, 6; Mary herself, 4, written down as "Eveline"; and the baby Burneice — Bernice — not yet a year old. Vernie Lee married at fifteen, in June 1934, to Queen England, with her father standing surety on the bond; that register is the paper that names Mary's parents. Proven Later, half-brothers and half-sisters came through Carl's second family, with Elsie Ray (Polston) Pelston — eleven of them: Kenneth, Homer, Walter, Larry, Terry, Ronnie, Edith, Ruby, Myrtie, Sylvia, and Louise. Mary's own obituary names just two — "fond sister of Walter and Larry Pelston" — but the wider obituary set on both sides of the family corroborates the whole sibling picture, and Myrtie, in hers, calls Mary her half-sister outright. The eleven are half-siblings (Carl × Elsie); "sister" in her obituary is the family's word for it. Proven

The third woman in the farmyard photograph is the sisters' mother, Pearl Branham — Mary Pearl Branham, standing with three of her daughters: Bernice, Mary, and Vernie Lee Pelston. The family's own picture register writes it out: "Brenice, Mary, Pearl (mom), and Vernie Lee Pelston," and the fuller scan of this photograph carries her surname in its filename — Bernice-Mary-Pearl-Branham-VernieLee.

The Kentucky household did not hold. Carl and Pearl divorced4 in the 1930s — the fact is plain from the 1940 census, which finds Carl, 49, marked divorced, living back under his parents' roof, while Mary is living somewhere else entirely. Probable Mary's mother later married Jimmie Wooton — by 1950 the census finds Jimmy and Pearl Wooten, she aged 54, farming at Gradyville in Adair County, with Mary's sister Bernice, 20 and never married, as their stepdaughter in the house. Mary Pearl died in 1983 as Mary Pearl Wooten5. Probable

The census trail

Three census sheets catch Mary across twenty years: a four-year-old in her father's house, a fourteen-year-old stepdaughter in another man's house, and a twenty-four-year-old separated mother heading her own household in Chicago.6

The two James R.'s of this census are two different boys, and this file never conflates them: the grandson of 16 in Luther's house on Sheet 4-A, and the stepson of 6 in Wooton's house on Sheet 5-A.

Two things about this sheet were argued over for years, and both are now settled as far as the sheet itself can settle them. First, the relationship word: two earlier readings of Mary's entry conflicted — "Stp Daughter" against plain "Daughter." The high-resolution re-read of 15 October 2026 settles it: the enumerator wrote "Stp Daughter" for all three children, cleanly, with no overwriting. Proven And she was Jimmie Wooton's stepdaughter — never Carl's. The older claim that the 1940 census called her Carl's stepdaughter is disproven; Carl is on another sheet the same spring, divorced and living with his parents. Disproven The family's own statement, given the same evening, says it in five words: "Wooten is step dad. See prior census."

Second, the wife. The Pearl in this house, 31, is not Mary's mother. She is a younger Pearl — born about 1909–10, daughter of a "Joe Pelston" and a "Sissie (or Lissie) Pelston" per the register of her marriage to Jimmie Wooton at Columbia on 9 July 1937 — while Mary Pearl Branham, born 1897, became Jimmie's wife only later, by 1950. That is the lane's two-Pearls finding (26 September 2026), and it explains the household: Mary's mother had gone, a younger kinswoman-Pearl kept the house, and Mary and her little sister and brother lived there as the stepchildren. Probable — the ages, the 1937 register's parent names, and the 1950 sheet all line up. What the arrangement means for Mary is plain enough without it: at fourteen she was a stepdaughter in a rented farmhouse, her parents' marriage over.

In 1950 Mary is a head of household in Chicago: a separated mother of a four-year-old, working a factory bench forty hours a week and taking in lodgers. Her first marriage is over in everything but the paperwork — the census says "separated," and no divorce decree has ever been found. Within the year she married again.

Between the sheets there are gaps the censuses cannot fill: no record yet found fixes when Mary left Kentucky, and the state-level traces of her Chicago forties come from the marriage license and the 1950 sheet alone. Those gaps stand as gaps in the ledger below.

Chicago, and the Western Electric story

By the summer of 1944 Mary was in Chicago and about to be married. How she got there, and where she worked, the records mostly do not say. Her own telling of it survives in the family.

Her own telling, as the family carries it: Mary met Edward Dedo when both of them worked at Western Electric — the Hawthorne Works in Cicero. She told the family so herself.7

The timing of her move north is likewise unrecorded. She is in Cumberland County in April 1940, a stepdaughter of fourteen; she is in Chicago by 27 July 1944, when Cook County issued her marriage license. Somewhere in those four years — wartime years, when the Hawthorne Works was hiring by the thousand — she made the move north. The records in hand do not date the trip. Open

The wedding — 5 August 1944

On Saturday, 5 August 1944, Mary Pelston, 18, married Edward Joseph Dedo, 26, at St. Camillus Church, Chicago. The license survives as an image and has been read digit by digit. This is the best-documented day of her young life.

LicenseNo. 1522327, Cook County — issued 27 July 1944 by the image's own date; an Ancestry index says 24 July. The image is followed here, the mismatch left standing. Open

AgesEdward 26 · Mary 18

Shirley Sleiva. Copies of Mary's portrait traveled under the filename "Mary Meier at Shirley Sleiva's Wedding" — and the filename was right: the portrait is from Shirley's wedding, where Mary stood as a bridesmaid. The family's ruling of 19 October 2026, that it was Mary's own wedding, was corrected by Brent Price on 29 October 2026. Shirley was a friend of Mary's. When and where Shirley married, no record yet says. Open

Two households

Mary's first marriage, to Edward Dedo, gave her Barbara and was over within six years; no divorce decree has ever been found. In November 1950 she married Warren Meier, and that marriage lasted fifty-eight years.

Her daughter Barbara Sue Dedo was born 4 June 1945.16 Proven The open-field photograph below catches the young family whole, about 1948: Edward in his hat, Mary laughing, Barbara in a bonnet between them, already walking.

Barbara herself holds the only memory of that ground. Asked in October 2026 where it was, she did not know — "Maybe a park ball field. He liked to watch AAA baseball." When she was older, Edward took her to the games, and once a player gave her a cracked baseball bat. Proven as her own memory, given firsthand. The ball field stays her suggestion only; no record names the place, and this page does not either.

By April 1950 the marriage was finished in fact: the census calls Mary "separated," and Edward's own death certificate, decades later, lists him as divorced8. Probable

On 11 November 1950 Mary married Warren H. Meier9 in Cook County — license No. 2157987, issued 27 October 1950. Probable Warren was a Cicero-born Army Air Force veteran of the Second World War.

Two children came of the Meier marriage: Debra Lynn Meier, born 11 December 1954 in Berwyn, and Tim William Meier, born 2 October 1959 in Chicago, at whose Indiana home Mary would die fifty-five years later.17 Probable

North Riverside — the grandmother I knew

In 1952 the Meiers bought a house new: 8912 W. 24th Street10, North Riverside, from the Achilles Homes development, at $15,950. She owned it for the rest of her life. It is the house her grandchildren knew her in.

The offering itself survives. Achilles Homes advertised the house in the Berwyn Life of 7 May 1952: a one-and-a-half-story brick "expandable," fully decorated, full basement, a quarter-block to school, a new church being built nearby. The family kept the clipping — it is filed as "Ma and Pa's House!", Ma and Pa being Mary and Warren. Whether they bought it straight off the advertisement, Brent does not know: "I assume they bought new, but not sure." What is sure is the year, the price, and the address: the house in the ad is the house they lived in.

North Riverside and Berwyn run together in her records — the funeral homes, the church, the obituaries' datelines — the near-west-suburban world she had come to as a bride in 1944 and called home for the rest of her life. She owned the house on 24th Street from the 1952 purchase until her death in 2014. In her final years she lived with family in Indiana, to be cared for; the house stayed hers through all of it, and it is the house her grandson Brent had been visiting since he was a kid.

The censuses end in 1950, and the documents say least about the six decades after them; the family knows that stretch best. What fills it in the file is family memory: the house on 24th Street, Warren beside her, Barbara and Deb and Tim grown, grandchildren, and the eighteen great-grandchildren her obituary counts. The family's book of her, The Fearless Kentucky Girl, carries those memories in full.

Warren died 14 December 2008, age 88, of North Riverside, formerly of Berwyn; his Chicago Tribune obituary names him "beloved husband of Mary, nee Pelston," a veteran of the Army Air Force, buried from Kuratko-Nosek Funeral Home with a funeral at Oak Park Avenue Baptist Church in Berwyn, interment at Mount Emblem Cemetery. The cemetery itself confirms he lies in Section I, Lot 341, Grave 5.18 Proven Mary was widowed in 2008 — six years before her own death — and spent the last years of her life as his widow.

Arkansas and Indiana — the later-years addresses

Her death certificate gives one residence — 8912 W. 24th Street — and her life was anchored there. But the public-records indexes that track Americans address by address catch her name, and Warren's, in two other states across the last twenty-five years of her life.

In the early 1990s the trail runs to Craighead County, Arkansas. Mary's public record places her at 2313 Spring Creek in Jonesboro on 1 November 1991, and Warren's own index entries carry the same street. By 1994 both spouses appear at 3006 Highmeadow Drive in Jonesboro and at 1101 Estelle Street in Lake City, some twelve miles away — Warren's Lake City entry is dated 1 May 1994. Why they went south, the record does not say. The entries put both spouses at the same Jonesboro and Lake City addresses in those years. Probable (FamilySearch U.S. Public Records Index entries for Mary E. Meier and Warren H. Meier; Ancestry U.S. Public Records Index entries for Warren H. Meier, read October 2026.)

The Indiana trail runs nearer her children. Her record places her at 300 Franklin Avenue in Arcadia on 1 June 1997, and at 20917 Edgewater Drive in Noblesville on 13 November 2000. Her name also surfaces at 2177 Ledgewood Drive in Newburgh, at 1802 E. 241st Street in Cicero, and — as early as 1997 — at 600 S. Indiana Street in Atlanta, the street of her son Tim's home, where she would die in 2014. The Hamilton County addresses are where her children had settled.

None of this displaces 24th Street. The house stayed hers, Warren's record returns to North Riverside by 2007, and her death certificate still names the house as her residence. The indexes are capture records, not a diary: they prove her name was recorded at these addresses, not how long she stayed at each or why.15

The last years

The hair in her later-life photographs is a wig. Mary always wore one, as far back as her grandson Brent knew her.19 Proven

Mary Eveline Pelston Meier died on 22 April 2014, aged 88, at her son Tim's home in Atlanta, Hamilton County, Indiana11. Proven — Indiana death certificate No. 019113 names her, gives the birth date and place this page opens with, and names her parents, Carl Pelston and Pearl Branham. The same certificate gives her occupation as lithograph operator — a sharper name than the 1950 census's "bench assembly" for the factory work of her Chicago years. Her residence to the end was North Riverside.

The visitation was Saturday, 26 April 2014, at Joseph Nosek & Sons Funeral Home, 6716 W. 16th Street, Berwyn, with the chapel service at one o'clock and interment at Mt. Emblem Cemetery, 520 E. Grand Avenue, Elmhurst. She was buried beside Warren: Section I, Lot 341, Grave 6, next to his Grave 5. Proven — confirmed by the cemetery itself: Sofia Carrera Zoubi, Family Service Counselor at Mount Emblem Cemetery, wrote on 17 October 2026 that Mary E. Meier was buried next to her husband Warren Meier in Section I, Lot 341, Grave 6 in 2014, and that Warren was buried in Grave 5 in 2008.

What stands proved is plain: born in Cumberland County, Kentucky; a stepdaughter at fourteen; married in Chicago at eighteen; separated and working a factory bench at twenty-four; then a North Riverside wife, mother, and grandmother for the rest of her life; dead at eighty-eight at her son's home in Indiana. The gaps in her paper — a birth certificate, a divorce decree, a second license — stand as gaps.

Open questions

What this page leaves open, on purpose, until a record closes it.

  1. Her Kentucky birth certificate — the documentary completion, ordered in October 2026 and still in transit. It would paper her birth date, town, and parentage at vital-record grade. Until it is read, Burkesville stays probable.
  2. Pearl Wooton's death certificate — the standing decider for the two-Pearls question: its parent names and birth date settle outright which Pearl was Jimmie's wife in which years.
  3. The Dedo divorce decree — Cook County, sometime 1944–1950. No free index exists; the decree's date and grounds are unknown. Shared with Edward's page.
  4. The 1950 Meier license image — the index gives license 2157987, issued 27 Oct 1950, wedding 11 Nov 1950. Reading the image would lift the second marriage to proven and settle the "Meyers vs Meier" spelling that three Kentucky sibling obituaries carry.
  5. Shirley Sleiva — Mary's friend, at whose wedding Mary stood as a bridesmaid; when and where Shirley married is unrecorded. The complete 1950 ED pass (20 October 2026) found no Shirley Sleiva in ED 103-1399 — a Shirley M. Lange, age 3, on Sheet 9 is a different child — and no other Dedo or Rowe household stood in the ED.
  6. Florence or Mary, left or right — settled on 29 October 2026 at Brent's word: Mary left, Florence right, in the trio and in the lake photograph alike. What keeps the item here is only the check Brent promised with his mother, Barbara; if she adds anything, both captions follow.
  7. Western Electric — her telling stands; no personnel record has been found to test it, and none may survive.
  8. The 1930 neighbors — the Dwelling 231 household beside Carl's is now read, and it is her grandparents Luther and Bernie's. What remains open is the wider sweep: 1930 sheets 9-A through 12-A and 1940 sheets 5-B through 7-B are still unread, and Joe Pelston × Sissie/Lissie, young Jimmie Wooton in 1930, and Arnold Polston × Cora Piercy have not yet been searched there.
  9. The late-life portrait — its date, occasion, and possible memorial use are unproven.
  10. Birdie Stapp — 1940 Sheet 4-B: Rollin Stapp, 46, and his wife Birdie, 56 (born about 1884), a candidate for the "Birdie Pelston" sought as Jimmie Wooton's mother. The census gives no maiden name, so this stands as an unconfirmed lead only, never a fact. Open

Notes

  1. The middle name rests on the strongest authority this file has for anything about her: the family's own knowledge of her, confirmed on 24 September 2026 — "Mary's middle name is Eveline." The records agree in their shorthand way: her 2014 obituary and the 1950 census both give her as "Mary E.," the 1940 census writes her "Evelyn," and her siblings' obituaries call her "Eveline" and "Evelyn" in turn. A family note that says "Mary Elizabeth Pelston" belongs to a different woman — a Mary born in 1905 who died in 1990 — and is not merged with this one. Disproven as an identity for her. ↩
  2. That parentage is carried three ways at once: by the family's direct knowledge (a family ruling of 16 October 2026: "they are her parents — but don't have the paper trail"); by DNA, because Barbara Price's AncestryDNA kit shares 387 cM with Misti Pelston with Carl and Mary Pearl as the common ancestors, which Mary could not carry unless she was Carl's daughter; and by paper, because her sister Vernie Lee's 1934 Kentucky marriage register names the bride's parents outright as "C. D. Pelston and Pearl Branham Pelston." What is missing is only the paper that names Mary herself — her Kentucky birth certificate, ordered in October 2026 and still in transit. ↩
  3. The date is proven by the Kentucky Birth Index entry for Cumberland County, by her age of 88 in her 2014 obituary, and by her Indiana death certificate (No. 019113), which repeats it. Proven The place is graded one step lower: the index proves Cumberland County, and "Burkesville" — the county seat, and the place every tree and the family give — is probable until the certificate itself is read. Probable ↩
  4. The divorce record itself has never been found: Kentucky's divorce index starts in 1962, and eight targeted newspaper searches for a 1930s filing came back silent. Open ↩
  5. Her own death certificate, which would name her parents and settle several questions at once, is the lane's standing decider and has not yet been pulled. ↩

No two of the sheets write her name the same way: “Eveline” in 1930, “Evelyn Pelston” in 1940, “Mary E” Dedo in 1950 — the variant forms are the records’, and each panel below works from its own sheet’s spelling. One caution belongs to the 1930 form: the Ancestry index rendered the sheet’s “Eveline” as “Euylene,” the form this file long carried; the image re-reads — 26 September 2026, and again in the neighbor sweep of 20 October 2026 — read “Eveline” on the sheet itself, and the index form stands superseded. ↩
  7. Graded as what it is: her telling — family knowledge from the woman herself; no record proves it, and as a documentary fact it stands open. Open The 1944 marriage license lists no occupations. The Hawthorne Works' personnel files have never been found to search. What can be said is that the one employment record Mary does have — the 1950 census's "bench assembly," forty hours a week in manufacturing — is precisely the kind of work Western Electric's benches did, and the plant sat a short ride from where she lived and married. ↩
  8. But the divorce decree itself — the Cook County record that would date the ending — has never been found. Open It is an open item this page shares with Edward's: his page carries the same gap from the other side of the marriage. ↩

The "H." is all the records give for Warren's middle initial — "Henry," seen on some profiles, is unsourced and is not used here. Open ↩

The address is graded probable, not proven: it rests on address histories for both Mary and Warren, on a modern photograph of the house whose plaque reads 8912 (an earlier reading of "1013" was a misread, since corrected), and on the builder's own advertisement — Achilles Homes in the Berwyn Life of 7 May 1952, offering this address at $15,950; the clipping survives in the family files as "Ma and Pa's House!", Ma and Pa being Warren and Mary. That she owned the house until her death, her last years spent with family in Indiana, is her grandson Brent's firsthand knowledge, given 29 October 2026. Probable ↩
  11. An earlier tree entry put her death in North Riverside; that was the funeral-home town mistaken for the place of death, and it is corrected wherever this file controls the text. ↩

Daughters Bernie A., 24, and Elsie, 22, complete the house — and the standing fact the two censuses together make is that Luther and Bernie were Carl's near-neighbors in 1930 and his hosts in 1940. Probable ↩

The 10-year-old in Wooton's house fits Bernice — the baby Burneice of the 1930 sheet — by age and by household: she would be ten in the spring of 1940, and Carl and Pearl's younger children stand together here as Wooton's stepchildren. But the name as written is unsettled between this file's two image reads: the re-read of 15 October 2026 read the word as "Nice," and the neighbor sweep of 20 October 2026 read it as "Nute." The stepchildren line above prints the later read; the name-form itself stays open between the two, and the identification with Bernice is inference, not settled. Inference ↩
